strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely NLP/code-generation problem: evaluating whether LLMs can build modular, reusable code across multiple iterative turns.

The benchmark is comparatively large, with 5,258 Codeforces problems, and the proposed six-stage pipeline is designed to support continuous updates and reduce dependence on unvetted user-contributed solutions.

The combination of official editorials, Codeforces acceptance checks, AST-derived dependency structures, multi-turn and single-turn settings, and a broad set of closed- and open-source models provides a useful empirical foundation.
Average Pass Depth is a sensible diagnostic complement to coarse pass@k because it attempts to locate how far a model progresses through a dependency tree before failing.
The figures clearly illustrate the intended codeflow workflow, dependency decomposition, and pipeline, and the appendix includes prompt templates that will help eventual replication.
weaknesses: Core benchmark quality is not sufficiently validated. The solutions, decompositions, and natural-language subproblem descriptions are generated or reorganized by DeepSeek models, but the paper reports no human audit, filtering success rates, failure rates, or inter-annotator/model agreement.

Subproblem unit tests are obtained by tracing a single reference implementation, mainly on public Codeforces inputs. Such traces can be implementation-specific and provide weak edge-case coverage; no coverage, mutation-testing, or independent validation is provided. It is also unclear whether final model pass rates use hidden Codeforces tests or only local public tests.

The multi-turn evaluation protocol is underspecified. It is unclear whether later turns receive the model’s own earlier implementations or ground-truth helper functions, how failures and repairs are handled, whether failed turns terminate evaluation, and exactly which code and context are visible at each turn.

The multi-turn versus single-turn comparison is not tightly controlled. Performance differences may partly reflect fragmented context, longer interactions, prescribed interfaces, output ordering, or formatting burden rather than iterative code-reuse ability alone.

Experimental rigor is limited by evaluation on only the most recent 20% of problems, reliance on pass@1, missing confidence intervals or significance tests, and absent counts for long-turn and high-DSC buckets. Some claims about failure beyond six turns may therefore rest on very small samples.

The error analysis covers only two models, does not report the sample size, annotation guidelines, annotator training, or inter-annotator agreement, and uses potentially overlapping categories. The IR remediation rate is associational and does not establish a causal explanation.

The claim of being the first relevant benchmark is stronger than the evidence supports given prior multi-turn, interactive, and self-invoking-function benchmarks such as MTPB, InterCode, and CodeEvalPro. The transfer from competitive-programming function decomposition to real-world repository-level development is also not demonstrated.

Reproducibility is weakened by the statement that code and data will be available soon rather than providing an archived release, and the manuscript contains numerous grammatical errors, typos, and at least one stage-number mismatch in the figure captions.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important NLP/software-engineering problem: evaluating LLMs on multi-turn, iterative code generation with explicit reuse of previously implemented functions.
The benchmark is substantial in scale, with 5,258 Codeforces problems, official problem metadata and ratings, editorials, and an automated pipeline intended to support continuing updates.
Using accepted Codeforces submissions as reference solutions is a sensible quality-control step for top-level algorithmic correctness, stronger than relying only on artificially synthesized programs.

The AST-based dependency decomposition, paired multi-turn and single-turn settings, and structural labels such as depth and number of turns provide useful diagnostic dimensions beyond ordinary code-generation benchmarks.
Average Pass Depth is a reasonable attempt to localize where a multi-turn solution fails instead of relying only on a binary final pass@1 outcome.

The evaluation covers a broad range of closed-source, open-source, parameter-efficient, and reasoning-oriented models, and the reported trends across turns, depths, and model families are potentially informative.
The appendices provide examples of scraped problems, prompts, generated subproblems, and error cases, which helps readers understand the construction process.
weaknesses: The evaluation oracle is not sufficiently validated. As described, subproblem tests are input-output pairs captured by executing one reference implementation on public Codeforces samples, while top-level evaluation also appears to use public sample cases rather than the complete hidden Codeforces judge. These tests may have very low coverage and can permit solutions that pass examples but are incorrect.

Captured helper-function tests are relative to one reference implementation and its particular decomposition. Valid alternative modularizations, helper signatures, or data representations may be penalized, and acceptance of the reference solution does not establish that the generated subproblem specifications or unit tests are correct.

The benchmark is constructed using DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3, but models from the same DeepSeek family are also evaluated. This creates a possible bias or contamination concern because the decomposition style, descriptions, and reference code may favor those models; no independent audit or construction-model ablation is provided.

The multi-turn and single-turn conditions are not cleanly controlled. They differ in context, how much task information is released at once, accumulation of model-generated code, stopping behavior, and error propagation. The reported performance gap therefore cannot be attributed solely to difficulty with iterative code reuse.

A stronger multi-turn control is missing, such as providing oracle implementations of earlier helper functions, allowing repair after failed turns, or equalizing context length and prompt content. Without such ablations, the causal interpretation of the multi-turn gap remains weak.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a benchmark paper: the code and dataset are only said to be available soon, and the manuscript does not fully specify model versions, API dates, sampling parameters, number of samples, timeouts, test-case caps, prompt variants, filtering thresholds, or pipeline retention/drop rates.

The experiments use only the most recent 20% of problems, but the paper does not sufficiently characterize this subset, report confidence intervals or variance across runs, or establish the statistical significance of the model comparisons.

Codeforces contamination remains a serious concern. Although selecting recent problems may help, the paper does not report model cutoff dates, possible browsing behavior, exact problem date ranges, or systematic contamination checks.

The proposed Dependency Structure Complexity metric is only superficially justified: turns divided by depth is essentially a branching/width measure and does not necessarily measure semantic or dependency complexity. It is also confounded with problem rating and total number of turns.

Average Pass Depth requires more validation. Its raw values are difficult to compare across different dependency depths, and the score assigned after an early failure can still be large for deep problems. The paper does not show that APD correlates better with downstream ability or is more reliable than simpler metrics.

The manual error taxonomy and IR remediation analysis are preliminary. The sampled problem count, annotation guidelines, annotator backgrounds, adjudication process, and inter-annotator agreement are not reported, and only two models are analyzed.

The claims about real-world readability, extensibility, maintainability, and developer workflows are overstated. The tasks remain Python competitive-programming functions derived after the fact from a single solution, with no human developers, repository context, maintenance tasks, or empirical software-quality evaluation.

The claimed novelty as the first multi-turn iterative code-generation benchmark is overstated relative to prior work such as MTPB, InterCode, TreeInstruct, and CodeEvalPro. The paper needs a sharper empirically supported distinction rather than relying mainly on task difficulty.

Most problems have only one to three turns and an average depth of 1.94, while the long complex tail is small. The low pass rates may therefore largely reflect Codeforces problem difficulty rather than the ability to manage structurally complex multi-turn dependencies.

The writing contains many grammatical errors, typos, and formatting problems, including errors in prompts and appendices. A benchmark paper introducing a reusable data pipeline should meet a higher standard of clarity and technical polish.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important gap: multi-turn, dependency-aware code generation with reuse of previously implemented functions, rather than single-function or one-shot program synthesis.
The benchmark is sizable, with 5,258 Codeforces problems, and the paired multi-turn versus single-turn setting enables controlled comparison of model behavior on the same underlying problems.

The data pipeline is relatively ambitious: it uses official editorials, accepts only reference solutions that pass Codeforces verification, extracts function dependencies from ASTs, and is designed to support refreshing the dataset with new problems.
Structural labels such as turn count, dependency depth, and DSC, together with Average Pass Depth, provide more diagnostic information than coarse final pass@1 alone.

Experiments cover a broad range of closed-source, open-source, coding-specialized, and reasoning models, and consistently show a large multi-turn performance gap and degradation on structurally complex tasks.
The appendices include concrete pipeline examples, prompts, scraping details, and error cases, which improves transparency relative to many benchmark papers.
weaknesses: The evaluation oracle is the main validity concern. Subproblem tests are execution traces obtained by running the reference implementation on public Codeforces sample inputs, rather than independent or hidden unit tests. Such traces can have limited branch coverage, may encode implementation-specific behavior, and may reject alternative but correct helper implementations. The paper does not show that evaluated model code is submitted to the official Codeforces judge or validated against hidden tests.

The task decompositions and natural-language subproblem statements are generated by LLMs, but the paper provides no systematic human audit, inter-annotator assessment, or statistics describing malformed, unfaithful, or unnatural decompositions. Acceptance of the refactored reference solution does not by itself validate the quality of the resulting multi-turn tasks.

Reproducibility is not yet fully adequate: the code and dataset are only promised as 'available soon,' and no versioned repository URL is provided. Several experimental details are also underspecified, including exact model snapshots, decoding parameters, retry policy, execution environment, timeouts, and the number of manually annotated error cases.

The construct called 'iterative codeflow' is closer to staged dependency-based generation than to realistic iterative development. In the described protocol, a failed test stops the process, and the model does not appear to receive execution feedback, revise prior code, or negotiate requirements. This should be distinguished from interactive debugging or refinement settings.

The multi-turn and single-turn comparison may be confounded by differences in output length, context composition, and token budget. Additional controls, such as matched token budgets, oracle-provided helper functions, and reference-based continuation after a failure, would better isolate multi-turn code-reuse ability.

Only one pass@1 run on the most recent 20% of problems is reported, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated sampling. Several turn-count and DSC bins also contain very few solved examples, making trends in those bins unstable.

Average Pass Depth and DSC require stronger validation. First-failure depth remains sensitive to traversal order among same-depth nodes, while turns/depth is a breadth ratio and does not unambiguously represent dependency complexity. Correlations with difficulty, human judgments, or mutation-based fault detection would strengthen these metrics.

The error analysis covers only two models, omits sample sizes and annotation agreement, and the proposed IR remediation rate is descriptive rather than causal. Generalizability is also limited to Python, competitive-programming problems, and function-level tasks; the motivating claims about readability, maintainability, and real-world repository development are not directly measured.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored capability: dependency-aware, modular code generation in which new functions must reuse components implemented over several turns, rather than producing one monolithic solution.
The benchmark combines algorithmically complex Codeforces problems with real-world GitHub-derived tasks, giving both controlled reasoning challenges and broader software-engineering context.

The data-construction pipeline is substantial: it scrapes problems and editorials, generates and live-judge-validates modular Python solutions, parses ASTs, topologically orders dependencies, generates subproblem descriptions and tests, and labels structural complexity.

The proposed APD/APT diagnostics and DSC analysis go beyond coarse Pass@k by measuring how far models proceed through dependency structures, although their validity still depends on the underlying tests.

The evaluation covers 19 closed- and open-source models and reports consistent multi-turn degradation, depth-dependent scaling behavior, and a useful qualitative error taxonomy comprising incomplete reasoning, insufficient globalization, and instruction misinterpretation.

The authors include several quality-control measures: cross-model ablation of LLM-generated descriptions and decompositions, structural stability checks, human/subjective quality evaluation, stratified sampling of the 1,000-problem evaluation subset, compute-cost estimates, and detailed prompts in the appendices.
The paper is generally well organized and the appendices make the pipeline, metric definitions, dataset statistics, instruction templates, and error examples comparatively transparent.
weaknesses: The most serious validity concern is that, as described in Appendix A.5, CodeFlowBench-Comp model evaluation relies on public Codeforces sample tests, while subproblem tests are generated by executing the reference solution on those same public cases. Public samples have limited branch and edge-case coverage, so the reported Pass@1 and APD scores may contain false positives and may not establish full correctness. The paper should clarify whether final model solutions are submitted to the complete Codeforces judge; if not, hidden-test or live-judge evaluation is needed.

Subproblem behavior and unit tests are tightly coupled to one generated reference implementation. Helper functions are often semantically underdetermined, so tests derived from the canonical code may reject valid alternative decompositions or implementations. Mutation testing, multiple reference solutions, and coverage statistics would be needed to demonstrate that the tests are specification-based rather than implementation-specific.

The benchmark's notion of multi-turn development is narrow and mostly static. Functions are implemented in a predetermined bottom-up dependency order, with no changing requirements, debugging feedback, revision of earlier code, cross-turn error recovery, tool use, or agentic planning. Thus the claims about evaluating realistic iterative software workflows are broader than the actual construct; the task is closer to staged dependency completion.

The multi-turn versus single-turn comparison is not fully controlled. The settings differ in prompt organization, context accumulation, stopping policy after a failed turn, and the requirement to pass every subproblem sequentially. The observed degradation is therefore not attributable solely to multi-turn dependency reasoning.

CodeFlowBench-Repo remains small after filtering: only 70 multi-turn problems survive from 749 candidates, supplemented by single-turn examples. Its domain distribution is skewed toward System and Cryptography, and the heavy filtering introduces selection bias, limiting the strength of conclusions about real-world generalization.

Important statistical details are missing. The paper reports mainly Pass@1 and APD@1 without confidence intervals, bootstrap analyses, significance tests, numbers of independent samples, decoding seeds, or temperature settings. Differences between closely matched models may therefore not be reliable, especially on the small Repo subset.

The benchmark artifacts depend heavily on LLM-generated Python code and natural-language descriptions. Cross-model checks reduce but do not eliminate bias or contamination concerns, particularly because Codeforces solutions and GitHub repositories may appear in model training data. The human-quality and error analyses also lack reported sample sizes, annotation guidelines, and inter-annotator agreement.

Some novelty and positioning claims, including the repeated use of 'first' and the characterization of the setting as real-world iterative development, are overstated relative to prior multi-turn and interactive coding benchmarks. The Python-only design and conversion of Codeforces solutions further limit language and workflow generality.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and under-tested aspect of code generation: implementing dependency-ordered, reusable functions across multiple turns rather than producing a single standalone function.

The benchmark combines competitive-programming problems with repository-derived tasks, and the Codeforces component is substantial in scale, with 5,258 curated problems and an automated AST-based decomposition pipeline.
The empirical evaluation is broad in model coverage, comparing 19 closed- and open-source models across different scales and reporting both paired multi-turn and single-turn results.
The proposed turn- and depth-level diagnostics, including Pass Turn, Pass Depth, APT, APD, and DSC, are a useful direction for analyzing where models fail in dependency-structured generation.
The supplementary material provides considerable implementation detail, including pipeline diagrams, prompts, dataset statistics, construction cost, sampling checks, and error examples.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol has a major test-validity problem. For CodeFlowBench-Comp, model evaluation appears to rely mainly on public Codeforces sample tests; subproblem tests are input-output traces obtained by executing one LLM-generated reference solution on those samples. These tests are weak, implementation-specific, and may reject valid alternative helper implementations. Official tests validate the reference solution, but that does not make the model-evaluation test suite comprehensive.

The benchmark artifacts are largely LLM-generated: DeepSeek-R1 produces the canonical Python solutions and DeepSeek-V3 generates subproblem descriptions, while the same DeepSeek model families are subsequently evaluated. The paper does not adequately rule out generator-family bias, and there is no large-scale human-authored specification or test-set validation.

The central construct is narrower than the paper claims. The task is primarily fixed bottom-up function implementation in dependency order, not iterative real-world development with changing requirements, debugging, execution feedback, or revision of earlier code. A failed turn terminates the attempt, so the setup does not measure how models repair or refactor code.

The paired multi-turn versus single-turn comparison changes several factors at once: architectural freedom, context, error propagation, and the ability to coordinate functions. Without ablations such as receiving gold previous functions, receiving model-generated functions, or allowing revision, the reported degradation cannot be attributed cleanly to multi-turn dependency management.

There is a serious internal inconsistency in CodeFlowBench-Repo reporting. Appendix C.3 states that the final benchmark contains 70 multi-turn problems plus 12 single-turn problems, totaling 82, while Figure 15 and the main-text percentages imply 129 problems. The number of Repo instances used in Table 1 is therefore unclear.

Even accepting the larger count, CodeFlowBench-Repo is small and highly selected: only a small fraction of the 749 considered DomainEval problems survive, the Computation domain is excluded, and many tasks are shallow. This is insufficient for broad claims about real-world software engineering.

The structural analyses do not control for inherent problem difficulty. Turn count and dependency depth are correlated with official Codeforces ratings, so declines across turns or depths may reflect harder algorithms rather than dependency complexity alone. No regression adjustment, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided for the main comparisons.

The error taxonomy is under-documented. Table 3 reports percentages for only three models but does not specify sample sizes, sampling procedure, number of annotators, annotation guidelines in detail, or inter-annotator agreement.

Some metrics are conceptually unclear or insufficiently validated. In particular, Pass Depth is defined as D-d rather than raw depth, the table columns and depth conventions are difficult to interpret, and DSC is a turns-to-depth ratio whose relationship to dependency complexity is not convincingly established.

The 'first benchmark' claim is overstated relative to prior multi-turn, interactive, repository-level, and complex-instruction coding benchmarks such as MTPB, InterCode, SWE-Bench, and BigCodeBench. A more precise novelty claim and direct comparison are needed.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate: no accessible dataset/code URL or DOI is provided in the submission, several API-model versions and inference parameters are underspecified, and there is no systematic contamination analysis for Codeforces or GitHub-derived data.
The writing contains numerous typos, grammatical errors, and inconsistent terminology, which further reduce confidence in the benchmark's polish.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important gap: most code-generation benchmarks evaluate isolated functions or monolithic solutions, whereas CodeFlowBench explicitly targets dependency-aware, multi-turn implementation with reuse of previously implemented functions.

The dual-component design is complementary and well motivated: CodeFlowBench-Comp provides 5,258 algorithmically challenging, periodically updatable Codeforces tasks, while CodeFlowBench-Repo adds real-world GitHub-derived contexts across several domains.

The automated construction pipeline is substantial and reasonably documented. It combines editorial scraping, verified solution generation, AST-based dependency extraction, topological decomposition, test generation, and structural labeling, with appendices providing prompts, examples, ablations, and cost estimates.

Beyond Pass@k, the proposed Pass Turn, Pass Depth, APT, and APD diagnostics offer finer-grained information about where multi-turn generation fails and encourage evaluation of partial progress rather than only final success.

The empirical study is broad, evaluating 19 closed- and open-source models under matched multi-turn and single-turn settings. The consistent degradation with more turns and deeper dependencies, together with depth-wise and error-type analyses, provides useful insights into model limitations.

The authors make a visible effort to validate pipeline robustness, including LLM-ablation studies, human quality evaluation, stratified-sampling checks, and licensing/ethical discussion for Codeforces data.
weaknesses: Test adequacy is the most important unresolved concern. Subproblem tests are mainly obtained by instrumenting canonical solutions on public Codeforces cases, which may have low coverage and can accept incorrect helper functions. The paper should explicitly state whether final model predictions are evaluated against hidden/official tests or only public samples, and quantify test coverage or false-positive rates.

The benchmark has limited ecological resemblance to some real-world iterative development. Tasks are reverse-engineered from one canonical solution, use predetermined signatures and a bottom-up order, and stop after a failed turn; they do not allow revision, debugging, refactoring, top-down exploration, or alternative architectures. Thus, 'iterative codeflow' is operationalized fairly narrowly.

The multi-turn versus single-turn comparison is not fully controlled. Multi-turn requests provide different scaffolding and accumulate both context and earlier model errors, while failure stopping prevents later functions from being attempted. Oracle-prior-code, resume-after-failure, or repair experiments would help isolate whether the gap comes from dependency management, context use, or the evaluation protocol.

CodeFlowBench-Repo is much smaller and less broad than the main narrative suggests: only 70 multi-turn and 12 single-turn problems survive filtering from 749 candidates. This limits statistical power and generalization, especially given domain and repository selection bias.

Some structural metrics require stronger validation. APT can depend on an arbitrary topological ordering among same-depth functions, and DSC, defined as turns divided by depth, does not unambiguously measure dependency complexity because a broad shallow graph can have a high ratio. Confidence intervals and significance tests for the model comparisons are also largely absent.

LLM-generated natural-language descriptions and Python conversions may leak the intended algorithm or reflect model-specific biases. The ablations show stylistic/semantic consistency, but broader human verification details—including sample size, annotation procedure, and inter-annotator agreement—are limited.

Reproducibility would be improved by adding a direct artifact URL and more complete experimental details, such as decoding parameters, number of independent runs, context-length handling, time/memory limits, and exact closed-model versions used. Data contamination also warrants analysis because both Codeforces problems and high-star GitHub repositories are likely present in model pretraining data.

The 'first benchmark' positioning is somewhat strong and should more carefully distinguish prior multi-turn, interactive, and agentic coding benchmarks. A human baseline or estimated ceiling would also help interpret the low model scores and benchmark difficulty.
